key_concept: Facial (fac) and meridional (mer) isomers arise only in octahedral complexes of the type $[MA_3B_3]$ (monodentate ligands), where three identical ligands can occupy either one triangular face or one meridian (plane through the metal).
steps: Recall: fac–mer isomerism needs an octahedral complex with the general formula $[MA_3B_3]$. In the fac form the three A ligands lie on one face of the octahedron, all mutually cis at $90^\circ$. In the mer form they lie in one plane through the metal, with two of them trans at $180^\circ$.
Option (1): $[Cr(py)_3Cl_3]$ is of the type $[MA_3B_3]$ with $A = py$ and $B = Cl^-$. It therefore exists as both fac and mer isomers.
Option (2): $[Cr(H_2O)_6]^{3+}$ is $[MA_6]$. All six ligands are identical, so no geometrical isomerism is possible.
Option (3): $[Co(NH_3)_4(H_2O)_2]^{3+}$ is $[MA_4B_2]$. It shows only cis–trans isomerism, depending on whether the two $H_2O$ ligands are at $90^\circ$ or $180^\circ$.
Option (4): $[Ni(en)_2(H_2O)_2]^{2+}$ is $[M(AA)_2B_2]$. It shows cis–trans isomerism, and the cis form is also optically active. It does not show fac–mer isomerism.
Hence only $[Cr(py)_3Cl_3]$ has facial and meridional isomers.
why_not_others: $[MA_4B_2]$ and $[M(AA)_2B_2]$ show cis–trans isomerism, not fac–mer. $[MA_6]$ shows no geometrical isomerism at all.
common_trap: Students often treat any octahedral complex with geometrical isomers as having fac–mer forms, and so pick option (3) or (4), which show only cis–trans isomerism.
time_saving_tip: Look for a 3 + 3 split of monodentate ligands, i.e. the formula $[MA_3B_3]$. That pattern alone signals fac–mer isomerism.
